extracted.intended_audience: scientists, academic authors, and informed readers of Nature (book reviewers, editors, and science communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating and producing scientific books, treatises, and public-science communications (including organization, evidence, figures, references, and outreach). Useful for book reviewers and authors preparing scholarly or popular scientific works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science's mission and public communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should help rebuild civilisation not only by providing foundations for material progress but by introducing scientific methods and spirit into all fields of national significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote a much wider understanding of science; scientists and believers should undertake publicity campaigns (dozens of leaflets or short pamphlets) distributed widely to enlighten and stimulate public appreciation. Outreach materials should show concrete examples of what science means to industry and civilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and purpose of citizen science organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies with sufficient funds can perform valuable national service by active propaganda to extend understanding of scientific research and its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such organisations need not be scientific societies but groups of citizens united to apply scientific method to public life; they should watch and promote progress and secure funds to display national scientific achievements (e.g., exhibitions, 'Temple of Science').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broad, cogent observational evidence for scientific hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: A geological or large-scale scientific hypothesis must marshal diverse, cogent observations (geological, palaeontological, geodetical, stratigraphic) to support its claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims against multiple lines of evidence (e.g., fossil distributions like Glossopteris, stratigraphic similarities, coast fits). Avoid relying on superficial analogies; show that suggested contacts/continuities occurred at the appropriate times and with sufficient precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for alternative explanations and existing literature
rubrics_metrics.description: New hypotheses should explicitly consider and compare with competing mechanisms (e.g., vertical movements, isostasy, subsidence) and engage with prior work and critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how the new idea avoids or supersedes difficulties of established theories; cite and respond to relevant papers (e.g., Jeffreys on cooling effects, Brouwer on garland-isles). Do not ignore well-known alternative accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of global quantitative patterns to support theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorists should use global statistics and physical constraints (for example, distribution of ocean depths and land heights, isostatic principles) when arguing large-scale earth processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support qualitative claims with measured facts (the review cites ocean depths near 4700 m and land heights near 100 m as relevant evidence). Show how proposed mechanisms are consistent with known global measurements and physical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of ad hoc adjustments to fit data
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeatedly shift parameters (e.g., shifting the pole from point to point) merely to make the hypothesis fit disparate observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust theory should explain data without invoking arbitrary manipulations; be wary of explanations that 'press the hand of the master' on models to force agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and lucidity of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific writing should be admirably lucid and treat serious hypotheses with appropriate gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style matters: present bold ideas engagingly yet seriously; avoid treating important theories 'in the spirit of a jest' and strive for clear, readable prose that conveys the argument and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate organization for reference works vs textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatise intended as a reference work must be organized differently from a textbook meant to be read consecutively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alternate theoretical and experimental sections as in elementary texts; structure material to suit reference use (logical grouping, complete sections), so readers can find topics without following a prescribed reading order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and fidelity to original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A masterly treatise should abstract facts from original sources with minimal casual errors and comprehensive referencing to primary literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather information widely and accurately; ensure references allow tracing of quoted material to original sources rather than second-hand summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and diagrams must be accurate and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be technically correct, scaled appropriately, and, when historically significant, faithful to original apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly simplified or modernised diagrams when historical facsimiles would be informative; plot spectra on physically meaningful scales (e.g., wavelength); ensure crystallographic figures follow recognisable schemes and that blocks/panels are not printed wrongly or upside down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, traceable citation and referencing system
rubrics_metrics.description: References must be easy to find and unambiguous; grouping many distinct works under a single number that cannot be quickly mapped to text is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a citation system that lets readers find original sources without undue page-turning; avoid burying many references under a single numeral and ensure reference numbers are placed where the corresponding citation is discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an index for works meant as references
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference work lacking an index loses much of its usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the book is likely to be used for consultation, provide a comprehensive index (and correct pagination) in subsequent editions to facilitate lookup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abbreviations and excessive initials in narrative text
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations suited for tables or condensed abstracts irritate readers when used in narrative prose; repeating author initials excessively is distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve abbreviations for tabular or highly condensed contexts; use full words in narrative and avoid repeating initials when context makes the author clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation quality must not undermine content
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors of presentation (misplaced reference numbering, typographical errors, unfinished words, incorrect figure orientation) diminish a work's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous proofreading and careful production are essential; small editorial faults can distract users and reduce perceived reliability even when substantive content is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in using detrital mineral evidence for stratigraphical correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Detrital mineral compositions may be of limited, local significance and are often unsafe as the primary basis for broad stratigraphical correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize rarity and local provenance of detrital minerals; avoid broad generalisations from sparse data; substantial, patient fact-collecting across regions is required before asserting that mineral assemblages provide reliable correlation or paleogeographic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish applied motivation from scientific novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied or industrial problems can motivate pure scientific discoveries and should be acknowledged as legitimate sources of research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing or presenting work, note if significant advances arose from applied contexts (e.g., mine-air studies leading to physiological insights) and emphasise the interplay between applied problems and theoretical development.
